We sincerely thank the reviewer for carefully reading our paper. We greatly value the constructive feedback and insightful questions. Please note that, unless otherwise specified, the references cited in our responses align with those provided in the appendix.

1. Response to the reviewer's concerns in the "Weaknesses" section:

(a) In response to your suggestion, we will revise the introduction in the next version of the paper to make it clearer.

(b) As we do not have a convergence proof of the UBSR Q-learning algorithm, we initially decided to present UBSR Q-learning as a heuristic in Section 5. Following your suggestion, we will consider presenting all model-free algorithms in Section 4 when preparing the revision.

(c) The term "optimal risk'' refers to the risk value obtained by applying the algorithm aligned with the corresponding risk measure, whereas "expectile risk'' denotes the evaluation of policies generated under various risk measures using the expectile objective. Table 1 demonstrates that our algorithm successfully achieves the optimal risk under each respective risk measure, highlighting its effectiveness and consistency across different objectives. In line with your suggestion, we will include a detailed explanation of Table 1 in the revised version of the paper.

The comparative performance of the algorithms proposed in this paper under a common setting is presented in Section 5.1 (for RVI and MLMC Q-learning) and Appendix C.2 (for RVI and UBSR Q-learning). It is important to note that the OCE risk measure used in Section 5.1 is not a UBSR measure, which is why the UBSR Q-learning algorithm is not included in Figure 5.1. The comparisons involving MLMC and UBSR Q-learning algorithms are provided in Figure 5.2 and Table 3 (in Appendix C.2). We believe that these results clearly highlight the distinctive behaviors and strengths of our proposed methods.

2. Response to the reviewer's concerns in the "Questions" section:

(a) It has been established in the literature (see e.g Artzner et al., 1999) that coherent risk measures can be interpreted as distributionally robust optimization problems, and vice versa. This connection links our work to the distributionally robust MDP literature. We will rewrite this paragraph to clarify the connections with distributionally robust MDPs.

(b) Yes, it is well known that MDPs with static risk measure objectives suffer from time inconsistency, often resulting in optimal policies that are history-dependent. In contrast, the framework of dynamic risk measures provides a systematic approach to constructing time-consistent risk formulations, under which optimal stationary policies can be derived; see Ruszczynski 2010 for further details. This is the primary motivation for our focus on dynamic, rather than static, formulations of risk measures in this work.

(c) Assumption 2.12 (the Doeblin-type condition) imposes joint restrictions on both the underlying Markov chain and the chosen risk measure. This condition can be decomposed into two parts: Assumption 4.8, which requires a form of strong ergodicity of the Markov chain, and Assumption 4.9, which imposes boundedness on the slope of the loss or spectrum function when employing one of the three classes of risk measures considered in this work.

In applications, Assumption 4.9 can be verified based on the definition of the measure. Assumption 4.8 would be problem dependent. For example, in a machine replacement problem, it is usually reasonable to assume that the machine always has a positive probability of reaching the failure state. In an inventory problem, it is usually reasonable to assume that inventory could run out during any time step. Now it is true that both verifying and rejecting these assumption with statistical confidence could present a practical challenge. We expect future research to further explore how ergodicity in Markov chains applies statistically in real-world settings.

We finally note that one way of ensuring that 4.9 is satisfied consists in selecting a state as the reference state, and modifying the transition kernel so that any state action may lead to this reference state with $\epsilon>0$ probability. 

(d) The term "optimal risk'' refers to the risk value obtained by applying the algorithm aligned with the corresponding risk measure, whereas "expectile risk'' denotes the evaluation of policies generated under various risk measures using the expectile objective. Table 1 demonstrates that our algorithm successfully achieves the optimal risk under each respective risk measure, highlighting its effectiveness and consistency across different objectives. Following your suggestion, we will add a detailed clarification of Table 1 when preparing the revision.

References:  

P. Artzner, F. Delbaen, J. M. Eber, D. Heath. Coherent measures of risk. *Mathematical Finance*. 9(3):203-28, 1999.

3. Response to the reviewer's concerns in the "Minor comments/typos" section:

We implement the corrections, thank you for pointing out!

Please note that, unless otherwise specified, the references cited in our responses correspond to those included in the appendix.

1. Response to the reviewer's concerns in the "Weaknesses" section:

Incorporating risk measures introduces additional challenges beyond the risk-neutral setting, particularly in establishing a seminorm contraction property. To address this, Shen et al., 2013 proposed a Doeblin-type condition (Assumption 2.12), which provides a theoretical foundation for ensuring such seminorm contraction. However, these difficulties remain when extending the AROE framework to other classes of dynamic programming and RL algorithms. In response to your suggestion, we will include a more detailed discussion of the Doeblin-type condition in the next revision of the paper.

2. Response to the reviewer's concerns in the "Questions" section:

The treatment of discounting differs significantly depending on whether the discount factor $\gamma$ is applied directly to the cost function or to the risk measure. The former leads to a time-inconsistent dynamic risk measure and may induce non-stationary optimal policies, thereby complicating the analysis (also see the discussion in Section 5.1 of Shen et al., 2013). In contrast, applying discounting to the risk measure results in a time-consistent formulation. However, unlike the risk-neutral case, even for well-studied risk measures such as the entropic risk, the vanishing discount approach may fail to converge or may produce a different limit, as discussed in Jaskiewicz 2007. That work also provides sufficient conditions under which the vanishing discount method is valid for entropic risk measure. We conjecture that similar results may hold for other classes of risk measures under appropriate assumptions, but a thorough investigation is beyond the scope of this paper and is left for future research.

References: 

A. Jaskiewicz. Average optimality for risk-sensitive control with general state space. *The Annals of Applied Probability*, 17(2): 654-675, 2007.

3. Response to the reviewer's concerns in the "Limitations" section:

Following your suggestion, we will include a discussion on potential extensions to other RL algorithms as part of our future work in the revised version.

We sincerely thank the reviewer for their careful reading of our paper and for recognizing our contributions. We deeply appreciate the constructive feedback and insightful questions provided. Please note that, unless otherwise specified, the references cited in our responses are consistent with those listed in the appendix.

1. Response to the reviewer's concerns in the "Weaknesses" section:

(a) We understand the reviewers concern and will clarify the differences in applicability between the two Q-learning algorithms in the revised version of the paper (also see our response to "Question.(a)").

(b) Assumption 2.12 is the Doeblin-type condition. Intuitively, it ensures that certain states are visited infinitely often from any other state under all transition kernels induced by the risk map. For the three classes of risk measures considered in this work, this condition can be decomposed into two parts: Assumption 4.8, which requires a form of strong ergodicity of the Markov chain, and Assumption 4.9, which imposes boundedness on the slope of the loss or spectrum function. While this Doeblin-type condition is sufficient to guarantee the validity of the AROE, it is not necessary. We conjecture that the weaker conditions needed in the risk neutral setting might be sufficient for a broader class of risk measures.
    
On the contrary, Assumption 3.1 is a standard and relatively mild condition commonly used in the context of average-cost problems, see e.g. Abounadi et al., 2001; Wan et al., 2021. Note that Assumption 3.1 is not about the MDP itself, but rather provides flexibility in how the algorithm is implemented.

(c) In the model-based setting, we introduce the risk-aware RVI algorithm as a special case of the more general risk-aware RQI algorithm, differing only in that the value function is replaced by the Q-factor and we directly establish the proof of the risk-aware RQI. Consequently, we treat them as one algorithm.

In the model-free setting, we present a natural extension of the risk-aware RQI in the form of a MLMC-based Q-learning algorithm, for which we also established the convergence to optimality. As for the UBSR Q-learning algorithm, due to the lack of a theoretical convergence proof, we regard it as a heuristic approach. We assess its empirical performance by comparing it with the risk-aware RVI and MLMC Q-learning algorithms in the experimental section.

To avoid confusion, we will revise the introduction to clarify which three algorithms are being referred to.

(d) We wish to first respond to the comment "There are no comparisons to existing risk-sensitive RL algorithms." To the best of our knowledge, the only prior work proposing Q-learning algorithms for average risk-aware MDPs with dynamic risk measures has either focused on the risk-neutral setting, the entropic risk measure (Borkar, 2002), or indirectly addressed coherent risk measures (Wang et al., 2023c), as noted in our introduction. None of these prior works can be used as a benchmark when using the risk measures employed in our numerical study. We encourage the reviewer to further comment on potential benchmark that they might have in mind. As a side note, following reviewer RUxx's comment, we plan to add a comparison of the convergence speed of our algorithms with those used in the risk-neutral setting, which may address the reviewer's interest.

Regarding the source of confusion in the presentation of our result, we will make sure to address this issue in the revised version of the paper. 

2. Response to the reviewer's concerns in the "Minor Issues / Typos" section:

We adopt the corrections, thank you for pointing out!

3. Response to the reviewer's concerns in the "Questions" section:

(a) MLMC Q-learning can be applied to a broad class of dynamic risk measures, while requiring access to repeated samples of transitions from a given state-action pair (i.e. a simulator). In contrast, UBSR Q-learning more closely aligns with the traditional setting of Q-learning, but is dedicated to the specific class of dynamic UBSR measures.

We note that the convergence of UBSR is not formally proven compared to MLMC, although its rate of convergence appears faster empirically. As a result, UBSR Q-learning may be used to potentially achieve faster computation with dynamic UBSR, whereas MLMC Q-learning is recommended for broader applicability and theoretical guarantees.

(b) As discussed in our response to the "Weaknesses" section, Assumption 2.12 can be decomposed into two parts for the three classes of risk measures considered in this work: Assumption 4.8, which entails a form of strong ergodicity for the Markov chain, and Assumption 4.9, which requires boundedness of the slope of the loss or spectrum function. Assumption 4.8 might be considered the most limiting of the two. In an application, it can easily be satisfied by selecting a state as the reference state, and modifying the transition kernel so that any state action may lead to this reference state with $\epsilon>0$ probability. 

We also conjecture that weaker conditions may suffice for particular types of risk measures. For instance, in the risk-neutral case, the AROE holds under the milder unichain assumption on the underlying Markov chain.

In terms of checking these assumptions in an application, Assumption 4.9 can be verified based on the definition of the risk measure. Assumption 4.8 would be problem dependent. For example, in a machine replacement problem, it is usually reasonable to assume that the machine always has a positive probability of reaching the failure state. In an inventory problem, it is usually reasonable to assume that inventory could run out during any time step. Now it is true that both verifying or rejecting this assumption with confidence based on data could present a statistical challenge. We expect future research to further explore how ergodicity in Markov chains applies statistically in real-world settings.

(c) We use the risk-aware RVI algorithm. The risk-aware MLMC algorithm would produce similar results. Following your notice, we will add a line in the application section specifying the algorithm being used.

(d) The term "optimal risk'' refers to the risk value obtained by applying the algorithm aligned with the corresponding risk measure, whereas "expectile risk'' denotes the evaluation of policies generated under various risk measures using the expectile objective. Table 1 demonstrates that our algorithm successfully achieves the optimal risk under each respective risk measure, highlighting its effectiveness and consistency across different objectives.

(e) We attempted to establish the convergence of the UBSR Q-learning algorithm but encountered significant obstacles. The analysis appears to fall outside the scope of standard ODE-based stochastic approximation techniques. Further discussion of these difficulties can be found in the last paragraph of Section C.2.

(f) We believe that our algorithm holds potential for broader real-world applications. However, as is well known, the "curse of dimensionality'' poses significant challenges to the scalability of dynamic programming methods. As a direction for future work, we aim to develop approximate dynamic programming and deep reinforcement learning techniques to address this limitation.

4. Response to the reviewer's concerns in the "Limitation" section:

Following your advice, we will add a discussion of extension to high-dimensional cases as a future work in our conclusion part.

rebuttal.value:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for their thorough review of our paper and for acknowledging our contributions. We are truly grateful for the constructive feedback and thoughtful questions. Please note that, unless otherwise indicated, the references mentioned in our responses align with those listed in the appendix.

1. Response to the reviewer's concerns in the "Weaknesses" section:

(a) Handling large-scale MDPs remains a central challenge in reinforcement learning, primarily due to the well-known "curse of dimensionality" that limits the scalability of dynamic programming approaches. Although the instances considered in our experiments are relatively modest in scale, we believe that the selected number of states and actions is sufficient to illustrate the validity of our theoretical findings. For example, in the convergence study, we employ randomly generated MDPs with 10 states and 5 actions per state; in the machine replacement setting, we consider a system with 30 degradation states. Developing approximate dynamic programming and deep reinforcement learning frameworks capable of handling significantly larger state and action spaces remains an important direction for our future research.

(b) As noted in the paper, establishing a theoretical convergence guarantee for the UBSR Q-learning algorithm remains indeed an open problem. Resolving this question will require further investigation and the development of new mathematical tools.

2. Response to the reviewer's concerns in the "Minor remarks" section:

We will follow the reviewer's advice and clarify this aspect by changing line 56 as: "We propose a model-based RVI algorithm for average risk-aware MDPs".

3. Response to the reviewer's concerns in the "Questions" section:

(a) The Doeblin-type condition imposes joint restrictions on both the underlying Markov chain and the chosen risk measure. Intuitively, it ensures that certain states are visited infinitely often from any other state under all transition kernels induced by the risk map. For the three classes of risk measures considered in this work, this condition can be decomposed into two parts: Assumption 4.8, which requires a form of strong ergodicity of the Markov chain, and Assumption 4.9, which imposes boundedness on the slope of the loss or spectrum function. While this Doeblin-type condition is sufficient to guarantee the validity of the AROE, it is not necessary.  We conjecture that the weaker conditions needed in the risk neutral setting might be sufficient for a broader class of risk measures.

(b) It has been established that more general time-inconsistent risk measures can give rise to optimal policies that are history-dependent and potentially stochastic. This significantly complicates the analysis, as it is unclear how an AROE of the type used in this work could hold in such settings. Addressing this issue remains an open question in the study of average risk-aware MDPs.

(c) To begin with, based on our understanding of the risk-aware RL literature, we respectfully disagree with the claim that static risk measures are the commonly used approach. Static risk measures, such as CVaR and VaR, exhibit time inconsistency, which often make the optimal policy history-dependent and unexplainable at a future point in time (see, e.g., section 2.2 in Marzban et al., 2023). In contrast, dynamic risk measures offer a principled framework for constructing time-consistent formulations; see Ruszczynski 2010 for further elaboration. For this reason, our analysis is grounded in the dynamic risk measure framework, and we do not aim to address problems defined under static risk objectives.  As you have noted that dynamic risk measures are generally not suitable as approximations of static risk measures.  For this reason, we have not tried comparing the values obtained from the two types of risk measures but agree that the question is worth further investigation.

(d) Following the reviewer's advice, we will include a figure and a discussion in the appendix comparing the convergence speed of our algorithms in the risk-aware versus risk-neutral setting. For the UBSR Q-learning, we remark that the risk neutral setting exhibits faster convergence rate.

summary.value: This paper studies the problem of solving Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) under average cost criteria when using general dynamic risk measures. In the planning setting, the authors introduce a relative value iteration (RVI) algorithm that accommodates an extremely broad class of one-step risk mapping. In the learning setting, they extend both multi-level Monte Carlo (MLMC) techniques and an asynchronous simulation-based algorithm tailored to the UBSR (Upper Bound on Sample Risk) framework. The theoretical developments are supported by a set of computational experiments showing the practical behaviour of these methods.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
**Strengths**:
- Well written paper with a comprehensive review of the literature.
- Strong theoretical contribution with rigorous proofs.
- Detailed experiments that support the relevance of the algorithms.

**Weaknesses**:
- The experiments only consider relatively small scale MDPs.
- The convergence of one algorithm (UBSR Q-learning) is not addressed.

**Minor remarks**:
- On page2 (introduction), it would be beneficial if the authors explicitly mentioned that their planning contributions (Section 3) involve model-based algorithms. The current wording might lead readers to think previous work was model-based, and this paper only introduces model-free methods.

questions.value:
- The results are heavily on Doeblin condition. Is there any intuition beyond this assumption?

- The results are based on time-consistent, monetary risk measures assumption. What challenges arise if one tries to handle more general, possibly time-inconsistent objectives (e.g. mean–variance)?

- The objective is designed with dynamic risk measures, which quite differs from the usual static risk measures. The dynamic versions are known to provide poor approximations of the static one and is generally harder to interpret [1]. Have you tried to evaluate this in the setting of average reward MDPs, in the environment you consider?

- How does the convergence speed compares to risk-neutral setting?

[1]  D. A. Iancu, M. Petrik, and D. Subramanian. Tight approximations of dynamic risk measures. Mathematics of Operations Research, 40(3):655–682, 2015.

summary.value: This paper addresses the problem of planning in average-cost MDPs with general dynamic risk measures. The authors propose three algorithms: a model-based risk-aware relative value iteration (RVI) algorithm, a model-free Q learning algorithm generalizing MLMC, and a model-free asynchronous off-policy algorithm for UBSR measures. The authors show theoretical convergence for RVI and MLMC-based, while the last algorithm is evaluated empirically on three problems: machine replacement, water reservoir management, and inventory management.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
*Strengths:*
The paper addresses an important problem by addressing average-cost MDPs with a broad class of dynamic risk measures. The introduced algorithms are novel and of practical relevance. For two algorithms, there are rigorous formal proofs for convergence (I could not verify them in detail, though). Generally, the paper is well-written and organized.

*Weaknesses:*
Convergence of the UBSR algorithm is only shown empirically, though this seems to be the most important one. The differences in applicability between the proposed algorithms could be stated more clearly in the introduction (under which circumstances, which algorithm should one use). Assumptions 2.12 and 3.1 seem quite restricting to me. While the paper presents one model-based and two model-free algorithms, section 3 "model-based algorithms" introduces two algorithms, section 4 "model-free algorithms" just one algorithm, which is confusing to me.
I see the main issue with this paper in the evaluation. The application to practical problems (machine replacement, water reservoir management, inventory management) is only briefly discussed, and all these systems are very small (and this limitation is not discussed). I do not understand which of the algorithms is applied for the results in Table 1 and why not all of them are applied. The results are not discussed at all, just some numbers are stated that "confirm [their] theory, proving [their] effectiveness". There is (almost) no qualitative discussion of the results, showing that the problem formulations and the solutions provided by the algorithms are sensible. At least, in C4 there are average costs of simulated trajectories for the inventory management problem provided, but this also lacks a detailed discussion besides stating that "the risk-averse policy produces trajectories with lower variance". It is also not clear there how the risk-averse policy is computed. There are no comparisons to existing risk-sensitive RL algorithms. Furthermore, the numerous abbreviations are confusing, e.g., for tasks. In many places, such as the discussion in the appendix, there would be enough space to state the full task title, which would enhance comprehensibility.

*Minor Issues / Typos*
- L. 8 "utility-based"
- L. 24 "MDPs"
- L. 81 "the the"
- L. 101 "in the follows"
- L. 147 
- L. 248 "a"

summary.value:
This paper studies the risk-aware average-cost MDPs, including the formulation of the Bellman equation, the required assumptions for the problem to be well-posed, and the formulation of the Q-function to be used for model-free reinforcement learning. Essentially, these are the theoretical foundations for RL algorithms to be used in risk-aware average-cost MDPs. 

There are papers studying a special type of risk-aware measures in average-cost MDPs, and this paper generalizes the risk measures that can be used.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths
- I enjoy reading the paper because it is very well written. The concepts, notation, analyses, and results are clearly presented. 
- The discussion on the connection to the literature is very thorough. My understanding is that risk-aware finite-horizon or discounted MDPs have been studied; risk-neural average-cost MDPs have been studied; and this is one of the first papers that studies the general risk-aware average-cost MDPs. 

Weaknesses
- I wish there are more discussions on the challenges in the formulation and analyses of risk-aware average-cost MDPs. It is understood that the average-cost formulation is harder to analyze than the discounted, due to a lack of contraction. What additional difficulties are introduced when risk-aware objectives are introduced versus the risk-neutral version? Will the challenges persist for other classes of RL algorithms such as value/policy approximation, policy gradient, etc? Such a discussion can help position this paper and its contribution.

questions.value: I have one question: in the analysis of average-cost MDPs, many of the studies use a limit argument. That is, use the discounted formulation and then take the discount factor to 1. This paper doesn't use this type of analysis. Why is that and what type of results would need such an analysis?

limitations.value: - The paper doesn't investigate other types of RL algorithms and discuss their applicability in the risk-aware average-cost setting.

summary.value: The paper addresses risk-aware average MDPs. First, the authors propose a risk-aware relative value iteration algorithm (model-based) to solve average risk-aware MDPs when considering dynamic risk measures. Then, the authors introduce two model-free algorithms and theoretically analyze them. The authors empirically show the algorithms converge to the right quantities and run them in three environments considered by previous works in the field of risk-aware MDPs.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
The clarity of the paper could be improved, particularly in the introduction. There are some sentences that are a bit unclear. E.g. "(...) the randomness of the environment is usually unknown, highlighting the importance of developing model-free learning algorithms." (line 37-38). However, I do not believe this should be a reason to reject the paper, but I ask the authors to review their introduction. The contributions are clearly stated. The assumptions are stated and discussed thoughout the document.

The organization of the paper could be slightly improved. In particular, I suggest moving Sec. 5.2 (which introduces a new method) to Sec. 4, and keep only the experiments in Sec. 5.

The experimental section of the paper (and respective discussion) should be further extended. First, in Tab. 1, I did not understand what is the exact difference between the "optimal risk" and the "expectile risk" column. Could the authors clarify? Maybe this should be made clearer in the text. Second, since the authors propose multiple algorithms, why don't the authors run them and show that they achieve similar performances?

The paper seems original, though I am not familiarized with the previous works cited.

Regarding the quality and correctness of the paper, I cannot provide an accurate assessment of them as I am not familiarized with the previous works cited by the authors. The paper is quite technical and, here and there, I got a bit lost reading it, but I believe it was likely because I miss some background knowledge regarding some of the concepts used by the authors.

questions.value:
- What does the paragraph that starts in line 48 has to do with the present work? One thing is risk-awareness (risk-aware MDPs), other thing is robustness to unknown dynamics (distributionally robust MDPs). Please clarify it as it is not clear why such cited works matter for the context of risk-awareness.

- Maybe the authors could add a bit more about the differences between the dynamic risk measures considered in this work and standard risk measures applied to the random return yielded by the interaction between a given policy and the MDP. In the later setting it is known that Markovian policies do not suffice for optimality, so I was wondering if the authors could provide more details regarding the difference between the two formulations and why they decided to go with the former (i.e., why do they decided to consider dynamic risk measures).

- "Remark 2.15. Assumption 2.12 is a sufficient condition for the existence of an optimal average risk independent of the initial state and is stronger than the unichain assumption commonly used in risk neutral average MDPs." - How easy is it to verify whether this assumption holds in practical problems? I ask this question because even verifying whether the MDP is unichain is already a hard task.

- In Tab. 1, I did not understand what is the exact difference between the "optimal risk" and the "expectile risk" column. Could the authors clarify? 

Minor comments/typos:
- "The condition we impose for convergence are weak" -> "conditions"? (line 65); "In the follows, we (...)" (line 101).

limitations.value: The authors discuss the limitations of their assumptions throughout the work. Some of them are standard (e.g., step size assumptions), while others seem more stringent. Unfortunately, I lack the background knowledge to assess the impact of some of the assumptions used.

title.value: Planning and Learning in Average Risk-aware MDPs

TLDR.value: This work presents planning and learning algorithms for average-cost MDPs with dynamic risk measures.

abstract.value: For continuing tasks, average cost Markov decision processes have well-documented value and can be solved using efficient algorithms. However, it explicitly assumes that the agent is risk-neutral. In this work, we extend risk-neutral algorithms to accommodate the more general class of dynamic risk measures. Specifically, we propose a relative value iteration (RVI) algorithm for planning and design two model-free Q-learning algorithms, namely a generic algorithm based on the multi-level Monte Carlo (MLMC) method, and an off-policy algorithm dedicated to utility-based shortfall risk measures. Both the RVI and MLMC-based Q-learning algorithms are proven to converge to optimality. Numerical experiments validate our analysis, confirm empirically the convergence of the off-policy algorithm, and demonstrate that our approach enables the identification of policies that are finely tuned to the intricate risk-awareness of the agent that they serve.

checklist_confirmation.description: In order to improve the rigor and transparency of research submitted to and published at NeurIPS, authors are required to complete a paper checklist and include it in the paper PDF. supplementary_material.description: All supplementary material must be self-contained and zipped into a single file. Note that supplementary material will be visible to reviewers throughout and after the review period, and ensure all material is anonymized. The maximum file size is 100MB. Supplementary material can be updated until the supplementary material deadline (May 22)

financial_support.description: Optionally indicate one student author on the paper who would need financial support to attend and present at the conference if the paper is accepted (or leave blank if financial support is not needed). Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors.

reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/ ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).

responsible_reviewing.description: We acknowledge that every author on the program committee is obligated to conduct responsible reviewing according to the policy designed by the PC Chairs and relevant members of the organizing committee. **Failure to do so may result in desk rejection or other serious consequences.**
